newsitem.title: NORWAY: France, U.S. at loggerheads over NATO reform.
newsitem.headline: France, U.S. at loggerheads over NATO reform.

text.p: French Defence Minister Charles Millon threatened on Wednesday to abandon plans for a full return into NATO in a row with Washington over who should head the key southern region command in Europe.

The increasingly-serious dispute, which surfaced on the margins of an informal defence ministers' meeting in Norway, could derail attempts to overhaul NATO's command structures and plans to take in new members from eastern and central Europe.

France, noting that Washington holds the top two posts, says the senior command post in the southern and northern European commands should be rotated among the European allies to make the European identity in the Atlantic Alliance a reality.
Millon told reporters France considered the issue of "fundamental importance" and could put on hold its reentry into NATO's military wing, which it left in 1966 in a dispute over U.S. domination.

"If a certain number of conditions are not respected... France will stay in the position where she is now," Millon said on the sidelines of the Bergen meeting, dominated by discussions over a new NATO-led peace force for Bosnia in 1997.

France, which always remained as a political member of the alliance, said last December it was ready to return to all alliance structures, but has linked the move to the creation of a European voice within the transatlantic alliance.
The United States, which provides most of the alliance's military hardware, argues that it must keep the southern command given its large naval and air presence in the Mediterranean area.

"The United States view is that the continued arrangement under which a U.S. officer is the commander-in-chief of AfSouth (southern command) is important, even essential," U.S. Defence Under-Secretary Walter Slocombe told reporters.

Asked about French opposition, he added: "We think there is an opportunity for the alliance and for France because of France's willingness to consider coming back wholly into the military part of the alliance. Whether they decide to do that is obviously a decision for the French."
Analysts said the French position was simply a negotiating ploy and a response to domestic criticism that its rapprochement with the alliance was a foregone conclusion.
Several other European countries, while eager for a real voice within the alliance, have distanced themselves from the French demand.

British Defence Secretary Michael Portillo said great progress had been made on the reform issue in general and there was now broad agreement that the deputy to the Supreme Allied Commander in Europe (SACEUR) should be a European.

"Nothing is settled until everything is settled. There is an emerging consensus on appointing a deputy SACEUR who would be European and have very special European responsibilities," he told reporters.
Portillo said he saw no solution which would allow the southern command to be held by a European but that "leaves bags of opportunites for the Europeans to play a full part" in NATO.

"What the French are concerned to achieve is that if they commit their forces to NATO...they should be coming into a NATO in which the European security and defence identity is more evident," he said.
"I am absolutely convinced that all of those conditons are going to be met."
